The Cornwall GP example data

Source: vignettes/cornwall-data.Rmd
cornwall-data.Rmd

spax ships open data on general practice (GP) care in NHS Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, in south-west England, and the guides run on it. This page answers one question: what is in the example data? It introduces each object once: what it holds, how the objects fit together and what they cannot tell you. By the end you can load each one and build the inputs that the guides start from. Nothing needs downloading. The spax() interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change in later versions.

The page uses spax with terra for the grids, sf for the points and polygons, and dplyr and ggplot2 for tables and maps.

library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

Four objects load with spax, and two grids are read from files:

Object What it holds How to load it
cornwall_gp 55 GP practices: location, GP workforce and list size Loaded with spax
cornwall_lsoa 337 small areas: boundaries, population and registered residents Loaded with spax
cornwall_flows Registered residents by small area and practice Loaded with spax
cornwall_travel Travel minutes from each small area to each practice Loaded with spax
cornwall_pop.tif Population grid, about 1 km cells read_spax_example()
cornwall_gp_travel.tif Travel minutes from each grid cell to each practice read_spax_example()

Each object has a help page with every column, for example ?cornwall_gp.

Practices

cornwall_gp is an sf point layer in longitude and latitude (WGS 84, EPSG:4326), one row per practice; easting and northing give the British National Grid coordinates in metres. practice is the NHS practice code, which links the practices to the registrations and to the travel times. The code drops the geometry and shows the first practices.

gp <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)
gp |>
  select(practice, name, gp_fte_extg, gp_fte, list_size) |>
  head()
  practice                                name gp_fte_extg    gp_fte list_size
1   L82001             LANDER MEDICAL PRACTICE   10.298887 12.858887     19477
2   L82003                  PORT ISAAC SURGERY    4.693333  5.546667      8738
3   L82004 WADEBRIDGE & CAMEL ESTUARY PRACTICE    4.341333  5.194667      8045
4   L82006                      PENRYN SURGERY    7.973333  9.893333     20089
5   L82007            CAMELFORD MEDICAL CENTRE    2.888800  2.888800      6658
6   L82008             STRATTON MEDICAL CENTRE    4.670400  6.377067     10746

The guides use gp_fte_extg as supply, what each practice offers: full-time equivalent GPs (37.5 hours a week) excluding GPs in training, from the June 2026 workforce data. GPs in training are left out because they cluster in a few training practices. gp_fte includes them. list_size counts all patients registered at the practice. Each practice sits at its main site, so branch surgeries do not appear.

Small areas

cornwall_lsoa holds the 337 Lower layer Super Output Areas (LSOA 2021) as polygons in longitude and latitude (WGS 84, like the practices); each area’s population-weighted centroid is given in both systems, cent_lon and cent_lat and the British National Grid cent_x and cent_y. The areas are small, of 988 to 3,392 residents. Each has an ONS mid-2024 population estimate (pop, also by age band) and the number of its residents registered at any GP practice in England (registered). That number splits into residents registered at a practice in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly (registered_in) and those registered elsewhere (registered_out). The code adds up these columns and counts the areas in each broad rural-urban class.

areas <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_lsoa)

c(
  population = sum(areas$pop),
  registered = sum(areas$registered),
  registered_in = sum(areas$registered_in),
  registered_out = sum(areas$registered_out)
)
    population     registered  registered_in registered_out 
        585655         606796         601269           5527 
# Rural-urban classification (2021), in three broad groups
table(sub(":.*", "", areas$ruc21))

 Larger rural Smaller rural         Urban 
           81           103           153

registered_in and registered_out add up to registered. Registered residents outnumber the population estimate by about 4%, which reflects list inflation (patients who stay on a list after moving away) and the different reference dates. The map shows the small areas by broad rural-urban class, with the practices on top.

# Small areas with a broad rural-urban class
classed <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  mutate(class = sub(":.*", "", ruc21))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = classed,
    aes(fill = class),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(cornwall_lsoa), fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = cornwall_gp, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Rural-urban class",
    values = c(
      Urban = "#5b7fa6",
      `Larger rural` = "#a9c48f",
      `Smaller rural` = "#e3dca8"
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Small areas (LSOA 2021) and GP practices") +
  theme_void()

153 of the 337 areas are urban, but they cover little land: the towns show as tight blue clusters, and most of the county’s land lies in smaller rural areas. The Isles of Scilly are the small group of islands off the western tip.

Registrations

cornwall_flows counts the residents of each small area registered at each of the 55 practices, one row per pair with at least one registration. The code shows the first rows, checks that each area’s rows add up to its registered_in, and counts the pairs.

head(cornwall_flows)
       lsoa practice patients
1 E01018750   L82012     2185
2 E01018750   L82016       35
3 E01018750   L82025        1
4 E01018750   L82046        4
5 E01018750   L82066        1
6 E01018751   L82012     1691
# Each area's registrations add up to its registered_in
by_area <- tapply(cornwall_flows$patients, cornwall_flows$lsoa, sum)
all(by_area[areas$lsoa] == areas$registered_in)
[1] TRUE
c(
  pairs = nrow(cornwall_flows),
  registered_residents = sum(cornwall_flows$patients)
)
               pairs registered_residents 
                3188               601269

Every area’s rows add up to its registered_in, so the flows hold all 601,269 residents registered inside Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, spread over 3,188 area-practice pairs.

A registration is a stock: who is registered with which practice on one date (July 2026), not a count of visits. Residents counted in registered_out are registered with a practice outside Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, for example in Devon, so they are in cornwall_lsoa but not in these flows. The guides on the allocation model, a model of where each area’s residents register, fit it to these counts. The guides on floating catchment area (FCA) indices, which measure supply per resident, do not use them.

Travel times

cornwall_travel is a matrix of motorized travel minutes from each small area’s population-weighted centroid (rows, cornwall_lsoa$lsoa) to each practice’s main site (columns, cornwall_gp$practice). The code prints a corner of the matrix and summarizes the minutes from each area to its nearest practice.

cornwall_travel[1:3, 1:4]
          L82001 L82003 L82004 L82006
E01018750     67     49     46     78
E01018751     67     49     46     78
E01018752     68     49     47     79
# Minutes from each small area to its nearest practice
nearest <- apply(cornwall_travel, 1, min, na.rm = TRUE)
summary(nearest)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  1.000   1.000   1.000   2.564   3.000  13.000

The times are least-cost paths over a 2019 global map of the time needed to cross each cell of about 1 km (a friction surface). They are rounded to whole minutes, with a floor of one minute, so no time is 0. 197 of the 337 small areas have a practice at 1 minute. Traffic is not modeled. In towns several practices can share one cell, so they have the same travel time from every area. The map shows the time to the nearest practice.

# Join each area's nearest-practice time to its polygon
nearest_map <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  mutate(minutes = nearest[lsoa])

ggplot(nearest_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = minutes), color = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(cornwall_lsoa), fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Minutes", option = "magma", direction = -1) +
  labs(title = "Travel time to the nearest GP practice") +
  theme_void()

Most small areas are within a few minutes of a practice. The map gives most of its area to the large rural areas, so the many small town areas, mostly at 1 minute, are hard to see. The longest trips, up to 13 minutes, are at the western tip, inland in the north-east and in one area on the north coast near Padstow.

The grids

Two GeoTIFF files cover the same 30 arc-second grid (about 1 km, in longitude and latitude). cornwall_pop.tif holds WorldPop 2020 estimated residents per cell: a count, not a density. cornwall_gp_travel.tif holds one layer of travel minutes per practice, named by practice code. read_spax_example() reads both, and the code counts their cells, layers and residents.

pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")

c(
  cells = ncell(pop),
  populated_cells = sum(!is.na(values(pop))),
  travel_layers = nlyr(travel_grid),
  grid_residents = round(global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]),
  ons_residents = sum(areas$pop)
)
          cells populated_cells   travel_layers  grid_residents   ons_residents 
          35772            6985              55          542666          585655

The grid holds about 7% fewer residents than the ONS mid-2024 estimate in cornwall_lsoa. The two are different sources and dates: choose one for an analysis and say which. In the travel layers, NA marks cells with no residents, pairs with no road connection and journeys over 180 minutes. The map shows residents per cell in six classes.

# The outline of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly: the small areas share the
# grid's longitude and latitude (WGS 84)
outline <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  st_union() |>
  vect()

plot(
  pop,
  breaks = c(0, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 5000),
  col = hcl.colors(6, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE),
  axes = FALSE,
  main = "WorldPop 2020: residents per cell (about 1 km)",
  plg = list(title = "Residents")
)
lines(outline, lwd = 0.6)

Of the populated cells, 81% hold fewer than 50 residents, and the towns stand out with several hundred or more. The FCA guides use the grid, and the allocation guides use the registered residents of the small areas.

The Isles of Scilly and the mainland

The Isles of Scilly have one small area and one practice, St Mary’s Health Centre (L82017). Road travel times cannot cross the sea, so every travel time between the islands and the mainland is NA. The code counts the unknown times in the small-area matrix.

c(
  unknown = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel)),
  scilly_area = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel[areas$scilly, ])),
  scilly_practice = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel[, gp$scilly]))
)
        unknown     scilly_area scilly_practice 
            390              54             336

The unknown times are the Scilly area’s row (to the 54 mainland practices) and the Scilly practice’s column (from the 336 mainland areas). The islands do have access to the mainland, by boat and air, which these travel times do not represent. Rather than treat the islands as cut off, the guides model mainland Cornwall only: 336 small areas and 54 practices, selected with the scilly column. Mainland residents registered with the Scilly practice or outside Cornwall then count as registered outside mainland Cornwall. Bringing your own data shows what the unknown times do to an FCA index when the islands are kept.

The inputs used in the guides

The guides start from one of two short recipes, so that all of them model the same mainland. Both prepare the data with prep_data(), which lines the inputs up by ID for spax(), the function that runs a model on them.

A grid, for the FCA indices

An FCA index measures supply per resident, counting nearby practices more than distant ones. The FCA guides compute it on the population grid and the travel stack. The recipe keeps the mainland practices, then only the cells with a travel time to every one of them, so that no populated cell has an unknown travel time.

gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
grid_data
<spax data> raster 117 x 187 cells x 54 facilities; supply gp_fte_extg
  demand    1 layer; travel 54 layers
  note      holds terra rasters: prepare the data again after saveRDS()

[[gp$practice]] picks the travel layers of the mainland practices by name, in the table’s order. sum(travel_grid) is NA wherever any layer is NA, so the mask keeps exactly the cells with complete travel. trim() drops the empty margin the islands leave behind, and crop() cuts the travel stack to the trimmed grid.

The mainland grid holds 541,184 residents, against 542,666 in the full grid. As the print says, grid_data points to the rasters rather than copying them: run the recipe again in a new session instead of saving it.

Small areas, for the allocation model

The allocation model gives each small area’s residents a probability of registering at each practice, or with the outside option: a practice outside the data. It runs on numeric inputs named by ID: demand (the people of each small area who may register), supply by practice and the travel matrix between them. Demand is the registered residents of each area, so it counts the same people as the registrations. The mainland rows and columns of cornwall_travel have no unknown times. The labels in metadata record units and dates with the data. spax keeps them with every result and does not convert them.

areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")
d
<spax data> 336 origins (336 active) x 54 facilities
  demand      604,471 registered residents (July 2026)
  supply      GP FTE excluding GPs in training (June 2026)
  travel      minutes; unknown for 0 active origins
  policies    missing demand: error; missing travel: error
flows
<spax obs> flows: 3,188 origin-facility counts, total 601,269; loss poisson

d holds 336 small areas (origins) by 54 practices (facilities), all active, that is, with demand above zero. Their demand is larger than their registrations at mainland practices by 5,497 residents: those registered elsewhere, whom the outside option stands for. flows names its loss, Poisson, which is how a fit compares modeled with observed counts.

obs_flows() declares the observed registrations from the long table, which still includes the Isles of Scilly. When spax() fits a model, it matches the counts to the data and says in a message which counts it sets aside. Bringing your own data explains that message.

Sources, dates and licenses

Data Objects Source and date License
Registrations cornwall_gp, cornwall_lsoa, cornwall_flows NHS England, Patients Registered at a GP Practice, July 2026 Open Government Licence v3.0
GP workforce cornwall_gp NHS England, General Practice Workforce, 30 June 2026 Open Government Licence v3.0
Practice locations cornwall_gp ONS Postcode Directory, November 2025 Open Government Licence v3.0; contains OS and Royal Mail data
Boundaries, centroids, population cornwall_lsoa ONS LSOA 2021 boundaries and rural-urban classification, population-weighted centroids, mid-2024 population estimates Open Government Licence v3.0; contains OS data
Population grid cornwall_pop.tif WorldPop, 2020 UN-adjusted 1 km estimates Creative Commons Attribution 4.0
Travel times cornwall_travel, cornwall_gp_travel.tif Derived by the package author from the Malaria Atlas Project 2019 motorized friction surface (Weiss et al. 2020) Creative Commons Attribution (version 3.0 on the Malaria Atlas Project website, 4.0 in the Google Earth Engine catalogue; both permit sharing adapted data with attribution)

Each source keeps the license given in the table. The package’s MIT license covers its code only. The registrations and the workforce are from 2026, the population grid from 2020, the small-area population from mid-2024 and the road network from about 2019, so keep the dates in mind when reading results. The full attributions, with the required wording for each source, are installed with the package:

file.show(system.file("COPYRIGHTS", package = "spax"))
